# R2 Commentary 1:1–3 — Extraction Digest
**Range:** raw lines 1253–2097
**Coverage:** Text and commentary on Ecclesiastes 1:1 through 3:22, including Longman’s superscription/frame-narrator analysis; 1:2 *hebel*; prologue 1:3–11; autobiographical introduction 1:12 and quest 1:13–2:26; carpe diem 2:24–26; times poem and reflection 3:1–15; justice/death/animals 3:16–22; chapter summaries for 1 and 2; heading only for SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 3 (body of that summary not present in this slice).

## Claims

### C-R2-01 — Superscription by frame narrator, not Qohelet
**Locus:** L1255–L1257 (1:1)
**Quote/anchor:** "It is the opening line of an eleven-verse section that prepares the reader for what follows by setting the mood of Qohelet's thought. This introductory section was written by a second, unnamed wisdom teacher, whom I will refer to as the frame narrator"
**Claim:** Longman attributes 1:1 (and the introductory section 1:1–11) to a second, unnamed wisdom teacher (the “frame narrator”), not to Qohelet himself; the superscription introduces Qohelet’s speech in 1:12–12:7.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-02 — Superscription like title page; closest parallel Prov 1:1
**Locus:** L1259 (1:1)
**Quote/anchor:** "the one that is closest to the opening of Ecclesiastes is found in Proverbs 1:1: \"The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.\" The similarity may be part of the frame narrator's strategy of near identity between Qohelet and Solomon"
**Claim:** Longman reads the superscription on the model of prophetic/wisdom title pages (genre + authorship); its proximity to Prov 1:1 is intentional near-identity of Qohelet with Solomon, not full identity.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-03 — Superscription is second-hand work, not self-reference
**Locus:** L1263 (1:1)
**Quote/anchor:** "The most natural reading of the superscription in wisdom and prophetic literature is that it was added by a second, subsequent hand. … In my view, this superscription is the work of the frame narrator."
**Claim:** Longman rejects the view that the speaker wrote his own third-person superscription (defended only by a “mechanical view of biblical inspiration”); he assigns 1:1 to the frame narrator.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-04 — “Words” (dabar) introduces a speech/lecture tone
**Locus:** L1265 (1:1)
**Quote/anchor:** "it is safest to stick with the more general term \"words,\" since it introduces a speech. … Ecclesiastes 1:12-12:7 does carry the tone of a lecture of a teacher to his students."
**Claim:** Longman keeps *dabar* as “words” (not “events”); Qohelet’s body may be oral or written composition later used as foil by the second teacher instructing his son (12:12) against speculative thinking.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R2-05 — “Son of David” intentionally associates Qohelet with Solomon
**Locus:** L1269 (1:1)
**Quote/anchor:** "here it is beyond question that the superscription intends to associate Qohelet and Solomon."
**Claim:** Though *ben* can mean spiritual kinship without physical descent, here the superscription deliberately associates Qohelet with Solomon (purpose deferred to intro “Authorship”).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-06 — “King in Jerusalem”: Barton/Crenshaw vs grammar; Ginsberg rejected
**Locus:** L1271–L1273 (1:1)
**Quote/anchor:** "Both George Barton and James Crenshaw assert without argumentation that king in Jerusalem refers to Qohelet and not to David. … H. L. Ginsberg prefers a philological rather than a text-critical solution when he evokes a cognate from the Akkadian of Ugarit to translate \"property owner in Jerusalem.\" I do not find these and other efforts of comparative philology persuasive."
**Claim:** Longman notes grammar does not settle whether “king in Jerusalem” apposes David or Qohelet (issue “hardly crucial”); rejects Ginsberg’s “property owner” and finds LXX’s “of Israel” unnecessary—variant formula “king in Jerusalem” is acceptable.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-07 — Prologue 1:2–11 is frame narrator; Qohelet speaks only from 1:12
**Locus:** L1277–L1281 (1:2–11)
**Quote/anchor:** "Two textual signals make it certain that we are not hearing Qohelet's voice yet. The first is the appearance of \"Qohelet said\" in v. 2. … Second, and perhaps more importantly, 1:12 bears a likeness to the opening phrase found in the genre of Akkadian autobiography … Only after that verse may we be certain that Qohelet himself is speaking."
**Claim:** Against commentators who start Qohelet at v. 4, Longman’s genre analysis places Qohelet’s speech from 1:12; 1:2’s “Qohelet said” and the Akkadian-autobiography pattern of 1:12 mark the frame narrator’s prologue.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-08 — Frame refrain 1:2 // 12:8 sets somber mood
**Locus:** L1279 (1:2)
**Quote/anchor:** "The author/narrator of Ecclesiastes reflects the somber tone of Qohelet's ultimate conclusion by both introducing and concluding Qohelet's speech with the same refrain: \"Completely meaningless, completely meaningless! Everything is meaningless!\" (1:2 and 12:8)."
**Claim:** The frame narrator bookends Qohelet’s speech with the *hebel* superlative refrain to set mood and summarize Qohelet’s ultimate conclusion.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-09 — Prologue judged prose, not poetry
**Locus:** L1283 (1:2–11)
**Quote/anchor:** "While there is a little parallelism in the prologue, it is my opinion that the prologue is prose since it lacks the heightened presence of the cluster of traits that defines poetry in Hebrew: parallelism, terseness, and wordplays."
**Claim:** Longman classifies 1:2–11 as prose despite some parallelism; the poetry/prose distinction is vexed book-wide.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-10 — *Hebel* superlative: “meaninglessness of meaninglessnesses”
**Locus:** L1305–L1311 (1:2)
**Quote/anchor:** "The phrase completely meaningless literally reads \"meaninglessness of meaninglessnesses,\" or more traditionally, \"vanity of vanities.\" … The superlative is formed by the use of the word twice in a construct relationship (habel h'balim)"
**Claim:** Longman rejects KJV “vanity” (now means self-pride); *habel hăbālîm* is a construct superlative (like Song of Songs, Holy of Holies), heightened by repetition and “Everything is meaningless”; frame narrator presents Qohelet’s judgment as excluding nothing, later qualified by Qohelet with “under the sun.”
**Wiki targets:** [[hebel]], [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-11 — Whybray: frame “oversimplified”; Longman rejects that expedient
**Locus:** L1313–L1315 (1:2)
**Quote/anchor:** "R.N.Whybray, for instance, states … that 1:2 and 12:8 \"form a framework for Qoheleth's sayings which is intended to leave the reader in no doubt about Qoheleth's negative attitude toward human life.\" He goes on, however, rightly to attribute these verses to a second hand, but wrongly to argue that this later editor \"misunderstood\" or at least \"oversimplified\" Qohelet's message."
**Claim:** Longman agrees the refrain is secondary but rejects Whybray’s (and similar “preacher of joy”) claim that the frame misunderstood/oversimplified Qohelet; the negative summary is faithful to Qohelet.
**Wiki targets:** [[hebel]], [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-12 — *Hebel* = “meaningless,” not primarily “temporary”
**Locus:** L1317–L1339 (1:2)
**Quote/anchor:** "As Qohelet uses the term, and as the frame narrator picks it up and summarizes Qohelet's thought with it, does it signify that \"everything is meaningless\" or that \"everything is temporary\"? … the best assessment of the book's overall message support \"meaningless\" as the meaning of hebel in Ecclesiastes."
**Claim:** Longman surveys extra-Ecclesiastes *hebel* (idols; parallels *šeqer*, *šāwʾ*, *rîq*, *kāzāb*) to argue “useless/meaningless” is primary; only a handful of passages *may* mean “temporary,” and even those are uncertain. LXX *mataiotēs* / Vulgate *vanitas* support “meaningless”; Rom 8:18 *mataiotēs* likely alludes. Context and whole-book theology (hermeneutical spiral) confirm “meaningless.” He allows possible context-by-context variation but takes “meaningless” as normative.
**Wiki targets:** [[hebel]], [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-13 — Rhetorical “What profit?” assumes no profit
**Locus:** L1343–L1349 (1:3)
**Quote/anchor:** "The question is asked merely for effect. No answer is expected, and none is needed because the answer is obvious. … There is no profit! If there is no meaning (v. 2), how could there be profit to labor?"
**Claim:** Frame narrator’s rhetorical question involves the reader; *yitrôn* (“profit”) is unique to Ecclesiastes in the OT (nine times), from *ytr* “to be left over”; *ʿml* is rendered “toil” for its negative connotation (drudgery/misery).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-14 — “Under the sun” restricts inquiry; Leupold rejected
**Locus:** L1351–L1355 (1:3)
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet thus restricts his remarks to terrestrial human activity and work. … Herbert Leupold answered this question affirmatively. He paraphrased Qohelet's statement in this way: \"Let us for the sake of argument momentarily rule out the higher things.\" I, however, deny that Qohelet is merely playing such a philosophical game and argue that he truly feels the pain and anxiety that he expresses so strongly."
**Claim:** “Under the sun” (29×; nowhere else in OT) marks restricted terrestrial scope; extrabiblical parallels (Elamite, Phoenician Tabnit/Eshmunazar, Gilgamesh) exist. Ranston’s Hellenistic-Greek argument is “now dated.” Longman rejects Leupold’s mere philosophical bracketing of the transcendent: Qohelet genuinely cannot take a transcendent yet immanent God into account; the phrase may also evoke “sweltering heat.”
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R2-15 — Generation (*dôr*): human vs nature cycles; Crenshaw both
**Locus:** L1359–L1371 (1:4)
**Quote/anchor:** "James Crenshaw is probably correct in saying that dor has both human and natural cycles in mind. It is impossible to be dogmatic one way or the other."
**Claim:** Traditional reading: human generations ephemeral vs permanent earth (Jerome’s irony). Ogden (1986): *dôr* = nature’s cycles; Fox: *hāʾāreṣ* = humanity, not physical world. Longman keeps usual go/come sequence (rejects Fox’s verb-order argument; Hertzberg on *bôʾ* as sun “setting”); prefers cyclicality/death-first *hālak*; sides with Crenshaw that both human and natural cycles are in view; *ʿôlām* “forever” = future as far as the mind can conceive.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-16 — Sun “pants”: negative toil, not eager joy
**Locus:** L1381–L1383 (1:5)
**Quote/anchor:** "In my opinion, the negative meaning is supported and was so understood by the Septuagint \"drags\" (helkei) and Targum \"crawls\" (styp)."
**Claim:** “Hurry around” = lit. pant (*šāʾap*); positive (eager) vs negative (exhaustion) senses are possible; Longman chooses negative monotony/toil of the sun’s cycle, with LXX/Targum support; “place” may evoke subterranean chamber (cf. Ps 19).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-17 — Wind in circles: Crenshaw “rut” vs Whybray “reliable”
**Locus:** L1385–L1389 (1:6)
**Quote/anchor:** "James Crenshaw correctly notes that the use of repetitive participles … gives a \"sense of being caught in a rut.\" R.N.Whybray, however, manages to eke out a positive message here. He argues, rather unpersuasively, that the wind here is reliable and not arbitrary"
**Claim:** Wind illustrates sameness within apparent change; delayed subject builds suspense; Longman accepts Crenshaw’s negative “rut” reading and rejects Whybray’s positive “reliable circuits”; N–S complements E–W of v. 5 without proving non-Egyptian setting.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-18 — Rivers/sea: futile cyclic motion; insatiable desire foreshadowed
**Locus:** L1393–L1401 (1:7)
**Quote/anchor:** "Either meaning does not change the principle that is clearly taught here: all this activity does nothing significant. … The unfilled sea is a metaphor that brings to the surface a theme that will now become explicit in the next verse, that is, that human experience is characterized by insatiable desire."
**Claim:** Rivers never fill the sea (Crenshaw suggests Dead Sea as possible illustration); whether water only pours in or also returns to source, activity achieves nothing; Ibn Ezra’s four-elements scheme is interesting but earth is setting not peer element; avoid speculative hydrology.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-19 — All things wearisome; eyes/ears never satisfied
**Locus:** L1405–L1413 (1:8)
**Quote/anchor:** "Despite Graham Ogden's valiant efforts, wearisome (yege 7m) has negative connotations. … Eyes may see much and ears hear constantly, but it is never enough"
**Claim:** Pivotal pessimistic pivot from nature’s illusory change to dull human experience; *dābār* = “things” (forces of nature), not “words” (Whybray); *yĕgēʿîm* negative (contra Ogden); rejects Galling/BHS emendation; weariness exceeds description.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-20 — “Nothing new under the sun” vs progressive spiral of OT historiography
**Locus:** L1415–L1427 (1:9)
**Quote/anchor:** "normative Hebrew historiography may be described as a progressive spiral, not a meaningless cycle. … Over against the normative biblical view stands the thought of Qohelet, as represented here by the frame narrator, that the past will perpetually repeat itself in the future"
**Claim:** Frame narrator presents history as futile sameness; contrasts with prophetic/redemptive “new” (Isa 43:19; Num 16:30) and with 2 Pet 3:3–5 scoffers; limiting observation to earth does **not** preserve orthodoxy because OT affirms God’s new acts on earth—Qohelet never admits them; efforts to limit “nothing new” or harmonize with Plato/Cajetan/Jerome are apologetic dodges.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R2-21 — Apparent novelty is forgetfulness; past and future without significance
**Locus:** L1429–L1445 (1:10–11)
**Quote/anchor:** "Thus, the verse rebuts the objection that new things take place on the earth by asserting that what appears new to people has happened before. They just forget about it. … The prologue concludes here on this depressing note."
**Claim:** Objection “Look, this is new!” is rebutted: already long ago; even real tech novelty does not change sinful humanity (Hengstenberg). *Kĕbār* is a “Mishnaism” (Fredericks admits) without forcing late date. V. 11: past and future generations forget; significance not in past, present, or future; *riʾšōnîm/ʾaḥărōnîm* more likely “things” than persons (contra Crenshaw’s gender argument).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-22 — Chapter 1 summary: frame prologue + Qohelet’s evil task
**Locus:** L1559–L1565 (SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 1)
**Quote/anchor:** "One of the main themes of these verses is the monotonous sameness of the world in spite of the illusion of change. … In this chapter, Qohelet reveals his disappointment with God. God has given humanity in general and Qohelet in particular \"an evil task\" (v. 13)."
**Claim:** Ch. 1 has two parts: frame prologue (1:1–11) with key refrains and monotony theme; Qohelet’s speech (1:12–18) anticipates failure via two proverbs (15, 18); God-given “evil task” shows disappointment with God.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-23 — 1:12: Solomonic royal fiction; *hāyîtî* “have been”
**Locus:** L1456–L1462 (1:12)
**Quote/anchor:** "This addition assures the reader that the speaker meant to indicate Solomon. Besides David, whose son Qohelet is, only Solomon ruled over Israel from Jerusalem"
**Claim:** 1:12 follows ANE autobiographical introduction patterns; perfect *hāyâ* debated (Targum Ashmodai demotion; royal-fiction signal; “have been and still is”); Longman renders English perfect “have been”; “over Israel in Jerusalem” locks the Solomonic indication.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R2-24 — Quest 1:13–2:26: pleasure, wisdom/folly, work; death empties achievements
**Locus:** L1464–L1466 (1:13–2:26)
**Quote/anchor:** "Nonetheless, the spectre of death hangs over his head, making empty his achievements and successes. At the end, he concludes that if this life offers anything at all, it is in the occasional moments of joy in the simple pleasures of life."
**Claim:** First major autobiographical section: vain search in pleasure, wisdom/folly, and work under death’s shadow; only residual hope is occasional simple pleasures.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-25 — “Evil task” God gave; *ʿinyān* = task, *raʿ* = “evil”
**Locus:** L1486–L1504 (1:13)
**Quote/anchor:** "In my opinion, these translations ill fit the acerbic attitude of Qohelet … evil is a translation more in keeping with Qohelet's subtle criticism of God throughout the book"
**Claim:** Qohelet’s comprehensive wisdom search (*dāraš* + *tûr* near-synonyms; spy-explore nuance of *tûr*) is called an “evil task” God imposed on humanity; NIV/NRSV softenings (“heavy burden,” “unhappy business”) rejected; *ʿinyān* from “be busy” not “affliction”; “under heaven” ≈ “under the sun.” Continuity with Proverbs wisdom tradition is broken by calling the task evil and later denying wisdom’s life-giving claim (Prov 8:35).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-26 — “Chasing the wind” reinforces *hebel*
**Locus:** L1512–L1516 (1:14)
**Quote/anchor:** "Whether it is \"chasing,\" \"striving after,\" \"feeding,\" or \"herding\" the wind (or for that matter \"vexation of spirit\"), the point is that life on earth is futile and frustrating. In this way, the phrase reinforces the conclusion that life is hebel, meaningless."
**Claim:** Despite root ambiguity of *rĕʿût/rʿyôn*, Hosea 12:2 parallelism supports “chases”; meaning is clear: futility. Empirical method: “I observed” without revelation.
**Wiki targets:** [[hebel]], [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-27 — Bent cannot be straightened: world fundamentally flawed by God’s will
**Locus:** L1518–L1528 (1:15)
**Quote/anchor:** "there is something fundamentally wrong with life on earth, and, since the world as it is has come about as a result of God's will (v. 13), there is absolutely nothing that humans can do about it."
**Claim:** Proverbial saying (parallel structure); “bent” not moral “crooked” (contra Ogden via Prov 12:8/Job 33:27)—context + 7:13 make God agent of bending; missing cannot be counted is a “truism” (Crenshaw).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

**Locus:** L1530–L1540 (1:16)
**Quote/anchor:** "if he cannot find meaning in or through wisdom, then who can? … The transparency of the connection with Solomon may be seen in the elusive manner by which Qohelet associates himself with that king. He never comes out and states he is Solomon"
**Claim:** Credentials boast serves argument via Solomonic fiction’s usefulness and intentional transparency; “over Jerusalem” predecessor problem shows loose association not strict ID; ancient readers would recognize the device.

### C-R2-29 — Wisdom search fails; wisdom adds frustration and pain (contra Proverbs)
**Locus:** L1544–L1556 (1:17–18)
**Quote/anchor:** "Proverbs emphasizes that wisdom brings joy and life. Qohelet begs to differ, complaining that it brings frustration and pain."

### C-R2-30 — Pleasure quest (2:1–11): self-oriented; conclusion announced first as *hebel*
**Locus:** L1567–L1597 (2:1–11)
**Quote/anchor:** "Even before narrating the exact contours of his quest, he tells us his conclusion: it is meaningless. … The pleasure that Qohelet explores is self-oriented."
**Claim:** Murphy: form is “reflection.” Qohelet tests pleasure/*śimḥâ* (sensual/material, not worship-joy); laughter is madness; no lasting meaning. Dialogue with personified mind (“Come on”).

### C-R2-31 — Wine experiment under “wisdom”; not mere connoisseurship
**Locus:** L1611–L1621 (2:3)

### C-R2-32 — Building projects: Solomonic fiction; Verheij’s failed Eden
**Locus:** L1623–L1637 (2:4–6)

### C-R2-33 — Wealth, music, sex/concubines as sensual experimentation

### C-R2-35 — Death levels wise and fool; relative profit of wisdom erased long-term
**Locus:** L1681–L1729 (2:12–16)
**Quote/anchor:** "Death renders all things, including wisdom, meaningless. … in v. 14b he introduces the idea of a common fate. That fate is death, and it comes to wise and fool alike, rendering wisdom meaningless in the long run."
**Claim:** Pivotal section: wisdom better than folly as light > darkness (eyes in head vs dark walk), but same *miqreh* (fate = death) awaits both; memory of neither endures; cuts traditional wisdom (and Ps 49:15 hope that Qohelet never expresses); Wisdom of Solomon 2:4 may correct Qohelet. 2:12b difficult (Fox: “makes no sense as it stands”); royal personage last explicit here; if king finds no meaning, no one will.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[proverbs]], [[book-of-job]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-36 — “I hated life”; *raʿ* as moral evil subtly accusing God
**Locus:** L1753–L1759 (2:17)
**Quote/anchor:** "I believe Qohelet here subtly accuses God of moral evil. … I hated life is a personal statement, but, since he does not particularize it to himself by saying \"my life,\" it has the force of suggestion to his readers as well."
**Claim:** Tragic conclusion: work evil → life hateful; everybody’s life worth hating. Whybray’s Job 3 / Ahithophel parallels are *unorthodox* wisdom; Proverbs embraces life; 9:4–6 only prefers life to death without affirming Proverbs’ passion; carpe diem passages to be weighed separately. “Evil to me” kept strong (not mere “distressing”).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[book-of-job]], [[proverbs]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-37 — Death renders toil meaningless: inheritance uncertainty
**Locus:** L1763–L1815 (2:18–21)
**Quote/anchor:** "Though never explicitly mentioned, the nemesis of death is carried over from the previous section: as it did with wisdom, death renders toil ultimately without meaning."
**Claim:** Hates toil under the sun because fruits go to “whomever” (not specifically Rehoboam—contra early Jewish reading); “Who knows” expresses “utter skepticism” (Crenshaw); fool may inherit; despair (*yāʾaš*; LXX “renounce” wrongly fed repentant-Solomon tradition); anecdote of skilled successful worker leaving *ḥēleq* to undeserving non-worker is “great evil” (strong moral outrage, not NIV “misfortune”); stranger more than normal son-inheritance.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-38 — Toil: day pain/frustration, night no rest; mechanical retribution challenged
**Locus:** L1817–L1831 (2:22–23)
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet's frustration arises out of his expectation that hard work should bring lasting reward. … In the tradition of the three friends of Job, Qohelet represents a mechanical reading of the Bible's retribution theology, which would include Deuteronomy as well as Proverbs."
**Claim:** Rhetorical “what do people get?” implies toil not worth effort; day *ʿinyān* with pain/frustration (cf. 1:18); nights minds do not rest; no present reward and doubt/denial of afterlife (3:18–22; 12:1–7). Qohelet expects Proverbs-style retribution but experience frustrates it; even Deut/Proverbs sound a “minor chord” that the world is not so clear-cut.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[book-of-job]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-39 — Carpe diem 2:24–26: resigned seizing of simple pleasures, not affirmation
**Locus:** L1833–L1857 (2:24–26)
**Quote/anchor:** "Here Qohelet advocates, though resignedly, pursuing what appears to be the simple pleasures of life. … In the darkness of a life that has no ultimate meaning, seize upon the temporal pleasures that lighten the burden. … He purposely avoids an unqualified positive statement such as \"This is good.\" Instead, he couches his language in a way that communicates his reluctance and his lack of enthusiasm."
**Claim:** First of carpe diem series (3:12–14; 3:22; 5:17–19; 8:15; 9:7–10). Formula *ʾên-ṭôb* = “nothing better” signals resignation for a fallen world, not enthusiasm. Eat, drink, enjoy toil = limited enjoyment (not ultimate satisfaction; not free license after 2:1–11). Even this is “from the hand of God”; Christian readers mis-hear benevolence—Qohelet is “not so sure of God” and does not count himself among the privileged (cf. 6:2). Enjoyment of toil is limited, not inconsistent with 2:17–23.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-40 — 2:26: “pleases/offensive” not moral retribution scheme
**Locus:** L1869–L1873 (2:26)
**Quote/anchor:** "Context, however, forbids this otherwise acceptable interpretation. … Why would Qohelet think it meaningless if good things happened to good people and bad things to bad? After all, throughout the book it is precisely the lack of connection between ethical behavior and reward that causes Qohelet so much frustration."
**Claim:** Against reading *ḥôṭeʾ* as “sinner” in moral retribution (Whybray’s dual-truth harmonization rejected), Longman (with Hertzberg, Fox, Crenshaw) takes nonmoral “offensive/displeasing”: God arbitrarily favors some with wisdom/knowledge/pleasure and burdens others with gathering for the favored—and *this too is hebel*. Contradicts 2:21 if moralized.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-41 — Chapter 2 summary: pleasure, wisdom, work fail; divine concession still *hebel*
**Locus:** L1876–L1878 (SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 2)
**Quote/anchor:** "The chapter then concludes with an exhortation to enjoy the lesser pleasures of life. After all, God does allow a privileged few to enjoy life. But that is no comfort to Qohelet, who regards even that divine concession as meaningless."
**Claim:** Ch. 2 search path: pleasure → wisdom (better than folly but death-nullified) → work (useless) → carpe diem for the few; even God’s gift of enjoyment is meaningless to Qohelet.

### C-R2-42 — Times poem 3:1–8: beauty obscures bleak message of human non-control
**Locus:** L1882–L1886, L1916–L1924 (3:1–8)
**Quote/anchor:** "The beauty of the poem, however, obscures its bleak message. … In the final analysis Qohelet powerfully expresses that everything is frustratingly out of the control of human beings."
**Claim:** ANE wisdom “proper time” theme (Prov 15:23; 26:4–5); poem uses infinitives, anaphora of *ʿēt*, meristic opposites; *zĕmān*/*ʿēt* ≈ specific points in time; *ḥēpeṣ* here “activity” not “pleasure”—etymology must not make the passage “upbeat.” List is descriptive of what happens under heaven, not prescriptive (no “good time” to die/lose).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-43 — Poem pairs: merisms of life’s spectrum; selected cruxes
**Locus:** L1926–L1970 (3:2–8)
**Quote/anchor:** "Once again, it is imporant to emphasize that the poem does not advocate these emotions/states/actions, but simply describes them as parts of the full spectrum of human experience."
**Claim:** Fourteen opposite pairs (completeness via merism). Born/die, plant/uproot: no control of start/finish. Kill/heal not exact opposites; no BHS emend of *hrg*. Emotions: cry/laugh, mourn/dance (personal→public). Stones: Whybray’s agricultural/military reading preferred over Midrash sexual reading (Gordis follows Midrash). Embrace: affection/greeting, not necessarily sex. Seek/lose, tear/sew, silence/speak (Gordis mourning context possible; 7b also wisdom “right time to speak”). Love/hate // war/peace chiastic nominal closure. Order sometimes flips positive/negative.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-45 — 3:11: eternity in the heart is frustration, not rest (Kaiser wrong)
**Locus:** L1980–L1998 (3:11)
**Quote/anchor:** "It is as if God is baiting or toying with his human creatures, giving them a desire for something that is well beyond their reach. … But Kaiser goes on to argue that Qohelet believes people can rest in God. In this he is wrong. Qohelet's compulsive \"drive to know\" leads to frustration and exasperation, not to rest."
**Claim:** “Hardest” verse but common words. God makes everything *yāpeh* (“appropriate/beautiful”) in its time—sounds positive after the poem—and places *ʿôlām* in human hearts; yet final clause: no one can discover God’s work from beginning to end. Genesis 1 allusions (*yāpeh* vs *ṭôb*; *ʿāśâ* vs *bārāʾ*; image-like *ʿôlām*) may signal lack of enthusiasm. *ʿôlām* = “eternity” preferred over “ignorance/world/course” (Ugaritic *glm* “dark” path rejected despite 12:14 *ʿlm*); Crenshaw’s four options surveyed. Jarick: *aiōn* in heart but veil prevents equality with God. Kaiser right about drive to know, wrong about rest in God.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-46 — 3:12–13 carpe diem again: resignation; gift Qohelet lacks
**Locus:** L2000–L2010 (3:12–13)
**Quote/anchor:** "The context and the language of the verse indicate that this conclusion is a statement of resignation, not enthusiasm. … from his frequent expressions of pain and frustration Qohelet did not himself feel that God granted him this gift"
**Claim:** Variant *ʾên-ṭôb* formula: best available is happiness/enjoyment (nonmoral *laʿăśôt ṭôb*, contra Fredericks’s moral reading). V. 13 specifies eat/drink/enjoy toil as God’s gift—even power to take the advice is divine (Crenshaw). Qohelet’s pain implies he is not among the gifted; feels unfairly treated; gift = anesthesia for fallen world’s problems.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-47 — 3:14: fear God as fright into submission, not pious awe
**Locus:** L2012–L2016 (3:14)
**Quote/anchor:** "In brief, though, Qohelet believes that God acts the way that he does to frighten people into submission, not to arouse a sense of respectful awe of his power and might."
**Claim:** What God does lasts forever; nothing addable/removable (proverbial; cf. Deut 4:2; 13:1; Prov 30:6; Sir 18:6). Purpose clause “that they might fear him”: commentators who read pious “fear of the LORD” ignore negative context (5:6; 7:18; 8:12–13; 12:13 separate). God freezes human situation; learn to put up with frustrating world.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[tremper-longman]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R2-48 — 3:15: God makes the same things happen over and over
**Locus:** L2018–L2024 (3:15)
**Quote/anchor:** "In other words of Qohelet, there is \"nothing new under the sun\" (1:9), thanks to God and the way he runs the world."
**Claim:** Echoes 1:9; past/present/future—nothing new. Idiom “God seeks what is sought” (near-synonym roots): not “the persecuted” (most versions) but Vulgate-aligned “God repeats what has passed” (Crenshaw’s option list). Section payoff: ordered times exist but humans cannot know them → frustration → settle for lesser pleasures only if God blesses (Qohelet implied among the unblessed).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R2-49 — 3:16–17: injustice in the courts; divine judgment asserted then undercut
**Locus:** L2026–L2060 (3:16–17)
**Quote/anchor:** "Thus, we have a tension, if not a simple contradiction, in Qohelet's thinking. Qohelet asserts his belief in divine retribution but does not allow a time for it, and he goes on in the next few verses to cast doubt on the concept of divine retribution itself."
**Claim:** New topic: no justice where expected (law court = place of judgment/righteousness becomes place of injustice); abrupt Hebrew = outrage. Abandons Solomonic persona (king would own justice failures). V. 17: traditional belief God will judge righteous and unjust, linked to “time for every activity” (3:1)—but humans cannot know that time; no clear eternal judgment day. Doubting wisdom teacher struggles with tradition vs experience.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R2-50 — Humans and animals: same death-fate; no afterlife certainty
**Locus:** L2062–L2090 (3:18–21)
**Quote/anchor:** "In short, this section is one of a number that indicate to us that Qohelet did not have a conception of the afterlife. … At the very least, then, Qohelet is frustrated with the unknowability of the afterlife, if not its existence."
**Claim:** God “tests” humans so they see they are like animals—commonality is death: one fate, one breath, no human advantage (*môtār* related to *yitrôn*); all dust to dust. Contra Whybray’s “completely traditional”: Gen 2/Ps 8 special human kinship and rule are sidelined—implicit departure from normative OT. “Who knows” whether human breath goes up and animal breath down: MT article-pointing turned question into statement (possibly Masoretic orthodoxy-smoothing); Kaiser’s non-interrogative *mî* is a “desperate” orthodoxy defense. Rhetorical question denies certainty, not necessarily possibility (Ginsburg/Rashbam).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R2-51 — 3:22: carpe diem again because future/afterlife unknown
**Locus:** L2092–L2094 (3:22)
**Quote/anchor:** "if justice cannot be found in the present (v. 16) or the future (vv. 18-21), then humans should take advantage of every opportunity for pleasure presented to them now. … these \"pleasures\" in the present life are simply the best that we can do under the circumstances."
**Claim:** Another carpe diem: rejoice in work as *ḥēleq*/reward; rhetorical “who can bring them to see what will happen after them?” expects negative answer—“after them” = after death (Gordis’s “petrified” earthly “afterwards” less likely). Motivated by limitation and uncertainty, not triumphal enjoyment.
